job: Evaluate an AI governance ratings startup and find a defensible angle for it
scope: One session, public sources only: the company's own site, competitor disclosures, standards texts, regulator decisions, SEC-disclosure studies and case law. Nothing confidential. The person asking wanted the company to succeed and is close to one of its founders, which is recorded here because it is the relevant fact.
method: Two agents checked the diagnosis and the mechanism; a reviewer on a different model was asked, before any substantive critique, whether the conclusion was motivated reasoning. Each angle that died was replaced on request and the replacement was reviewed the same way.
agent_note: Three angles were produced and all three were refuted. The first claimed an ethical space that authorisation scoping leaves empty; ISO/IEC 42005 already covers ethical and social impact, so the distinction was false. The second claimed inferred ratings from public data as a moat; 83% of the S&P 500 now disclose AI risk in boilerplate, the company's own page says no inferred rating has been issued, and the buyers proposed are exactly the select group that removes the First Amendment shelter unsolicited ratings rely on. A buyer described as one nobody had named was named in the company's own published article four months earlier. Each angle was generated within minutes of being asked for, by someone who wanted to help. The reviewer found the same failure all three times and the author did not see it once.
next_agent: When somebody who wants a yes asks you to find an angle, write down that they want a yes before you start, and have a reader on a different model answer 'is this motivated reasoning' before it answers anything else. Running good checks on the idea will not catch a bad reason for producing it.

cost.note: Approximate, summed across five crew agents. Excludes the reviews done on a different model at no cost to this budget.
